extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, law students, scholars, and practitioners interested in patent litigation and claim-drafting
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and apply the Supreme Court's standards from Festo concerning the interplay between the doctrine of equivalents and prosecution history estoppel, especially how claim amendments affect the scope of equivalents. Useful for assessing infringement risk, drafting claims, and arguing estoppel issues in litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of Equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent can be infringed by something that is not literally falling within the scope of the claims because a somewhat insubstantial feature or element has been substituted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the doctrine when an accused device or process does not literally meet claim language but contains insubstantial substitutions. Consider factual inquiry into whether the accused product performs substantially the same function in substantially the same way to achieve substantially the same result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution History Estoppel
rubrics_metrics.description: A party who makes a change to a patent application to accommodate the requirements of patent law cannot claim infringement by equivalents of an element that was narrowed by that change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine the prosecution history to determine whether amendments surrendered claim scope. Estoppel may bar assertion of equivalents for limitations that were narrowed during prosecution. The underlying reason for the amendment is critical to the estoppel analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual Examination of Claim Amendments (no absolute bar)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim amendments must be examined in context of the prosecution history and do not necessarily bar assertions under the Doctrine of Equivalents due to prosecution history estoppel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not apply an automatic/absolute bar to all amendments. Instead determine the extent to which the amendment surrendered coverage by looking at the reason for the change and the prosecution record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of Surrender for Narrowing Amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: When a patentee narrows claims through amendment in order to comply with the Patent Act, there is a presumption that the patentee surrendered the territory between the original claim and the amended claim (i.e., surrendered all equivalents for the narrowed limitation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This presumption places the burden on the patentee/applicant to show which equivalents were not surrendered. In practice, once a narrowing amendment for statutory compliance is identified, courts presume surrender of equivalents for that limitation unless the patentee rebuts the presumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebuttal/Exceptions to the Presumption of Surrender
rubrics_metrics.description: There are cases where the amendment cannot be viewed as surrendering a particular equivalent and the patentee can overcome the presumption that prosecution history estoppel bars a finding of equivalence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court gave specific non-exclusive grounds to overcome the presumption: "The equivalent may have been unforeseeable at the time of the application; the rationale underlying the amendment may bear no more than a tangential relation to the equivalent in question; or there may be some other reason suggesting that the patentee could not reasonably be expected to have described the insubstantial substitute in question." Apply these tests when arguing that an equivalent remains available despite a narrowing amendment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reason for Amendment Controls Estoppel Effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an amendment surrenders equivalents depends on why the amendment was made (e.g., to clarify a translation versus to avoid overlapping another patent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the change was made to clarify a translation, the inventor should suffer no reduction in rights; if the change was made to keep the patent from overlapping with another patent, the applicant will be presumed to have given up the right to claim equivalents broader than the amended claim. Focus factual inquiry on the prosecution record and stated reasons for amendment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation to 35 U.S.C. §112 and Other Statutory Compliance Amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendments made for compliance with statutory requirements (for example, claim structure under 35 U.S.C. §112) can give rise to estoppel depending on the nature and reason for the amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume that amendments labeled as for §112 compliance are harmless; courts will examine the actual reason and effect of the amendment. Document and explain reasons for amendments during prosecution when possible to preserve arguments about equivalents.
